questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^n$, let $\mathcal{B}=(\boldsymbol{b}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{b}_n)$ and $\mathcal{C}=(\boldsymbol{c}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{c}_n)$ be ordered bases and let $P=P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$ satisfy $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}=P[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ for every $\boldsymbol{x}$. What is the $j$-th column of $P$?
options: $[\boldsymbol{c}_j]_{\mathcal{B}}$, the new vector $\boldsymbol{c}_j$ described in the old basis
$\boldsymbol{c}_j$ as a column of standard entries, the $j$-th new basis vector
$\boldsymbol{b}_j$ itself, listed by its entries in the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$
$[\boldsymbol{b}_j]_{\mathcal{C}}$, the old vector $\boldsymbol{b}_j$ described in the new basis

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with ordered bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$, the transformation matrix $P$ satisfies $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}=P[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$. What does multiplying $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ by $P$ do to the vector $\boldsymbol{x}$ itself?
options: Nothing: $\boldsymbol{x}$ stays the same vector and only its list of coordinates changes
It moves $\boldsymbol{x}$ to a new vector, the image of $\boldsymbol{x}$ under a linear map
It projects $\boldsymbol{x}$ onto the span of the new basis vectors $\boldsymbol{c}_1,\boldsymbol{c}_2$
It rotates $\boldsymbol{x}$ through the angle between $\boldsymbol{b}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{c}_1$

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^n$, let $\boldsymbol{f}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{f}_n$ be a new basis and $F=(\boldsymbol{f}_1\ \cdots\ \boldsymbol{f}_n)$ the transformation matrix with these columns. Which matrix converts the standard coordinates $\boldsymbol{x}$ of a vector into its coordinates $\boldsymbol{y}$ in the new basis?
options: $F$, because its columns $\boldsymbol{f}_i$ form the new basis
$F^{\top}$, because its rows $\boldsymbol{f}_i^{\top}$ give the dot products
$(F^{\top})^{-1}$, because coordinates are read off the rows of $F$

questions.question: In a real vector space $V$, let $\mathcal{B}=(\boldsymbol{b}_1,\boldsymbol{b}_2,\boldsymbol{b}_3)$ be an ordered basis and $\mathcal{C}=(2\boldsymbol{b}_1,\boldsymbol{b}_2,\boldsymbol{b}_3)$. If $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=(x_1,x_2,x_3)^{\top}$, what is $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}$?

Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Which real $n\times n$ matrices $M$ equal $P_{\mathcal{E}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$ for some ordered basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$, that is, satisfy $\boldsymbol{x}=M[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ for every $\boldsymbol{x}$?
options: Exactly the invertible ones; $\mathcal{B}$ is their list of columns
Only orthogonal ones, whose columns are orthonormal vectors
Only those with determinant equal to $1$, which preserve volume
Every $n\times n$ matrix, since any $n$ columns define coordinates

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$, take the new basis $\boldsymbol{f}_1=(1,2)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{f}_2=(0,1)^{\top}$ and the vector $\boldsymbol{x}=(3,7)^{\top}$ in standard coordinates. What are the coordinates $\boldsymbol{y}$ of $\boldsymbol{x}$ in the new basis $(\boldsymbol{f}_1,\boldsymbol{f}_2)$?

In $\mathbb{R}^2$, take the new basis $\boldsymbol{f}_1=(1,1)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{f}_2=(2,3)^{\top}$, and suppose a vector has coordinates $\boldsymbol{y}=(2,-1)^{\top}$ in this basis. What is $\boldsymbol{x}$ in standard coordinates?

In $\mathbb{R}^2$, take the orthonormal new basis $\boldsymbol{f}_1=\tfrac{1}{5}(3,4)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{f}_2=\tfrac{1}{5}(-4,3)^{\top}$. What are the coordinates $\boldsymbol{y}$ of $\boldsymbol{x}=(5,5)^{\top}$ in this basis?

Let $\mathcal{B}=(\boldsymbol{b}_1,\boldsymbol{b}_2)$ and $\mathcal{C}=(\boldsymbol{c}_1,\boldsymbol{c}_2)$ be ordered bases of a two-dimensional space with $\boldsymbol{b}_1=\boldsymbol{c}_1+2\boldsymbol{c}_2$ and $\boldsymbol{b}_2=3\boldsymbol{c}_1-\boldsymbol{c}_2$. Which matrix $P$ satisfies $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}=P[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}$?

For bases $\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$, $P_{\mathcal{Y}\leftarrow\mathcal{X}}$ maps $\mathcal{X}$- to $\mathcal{Y}$-coordinates. If $P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $P_{\mathcal{D}\leftarrow\mathcal{C}}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, what is $P_{\mathcal{D}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$?

For two ordered bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$, $P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}=[I]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}$ is the matrix of the identity map taking $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates to $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates. When does it equal the identity matrix $I_n$?
options: Always, since the identity map sends each vector to itself
Whenever $\mathcal{C}$ has the same vectors as $\mathcal{B}$, in any order
Whenever $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are both orthonormal bases
Exactly when $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{B}$: the same vectors in the same order

questions.question: Let $T$ be a linear operator on $V$ with ordered bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$, let $[T]_{\mathcal{B}}$ and $[T]_{\mathcal{C}}$ be its matrices in each basis, and let $S=P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$ convert $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates into $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates. Which product equals $[T]_{\mathcal{B}}$?

Let $T\colon V\to W$ be linear with $\dim V=3$ and $\dim W=2$, let $\mathcal{B},\mathcal{B}'$ be bases of $V$ and $\mathcal{C}$ a basis of $W$, and let $[T]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}$ map $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates to $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates. If only the basis of $V$ changes to $\mathcal{B}'$, which product equals $[T]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}'}$?

The operator $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is given in standard coordinates. What is its matrix in the new basis $\boldsymbol{f}_1=(1,1)^{\top}$, $\boldsymbol{f}_2=(1,0)^{\top}$, used for both input and output?

In the space $P_1$ of real polynomials of degree at most $1$, take the ordered bases $\mathcal{B}=(1,t)$ and $\mathcal{C}=(1,1+t)$. Which matrix is $P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$, converting $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates into $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates?

For ordered bases $\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$, the transformation matrix $P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}=P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$. A vector has $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}=(1,1)^{\top}$. What is $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$?

In $\mathbb{R}^n$, let $F$ be the transformation matrix whose columns are the new basis vectors $\boldsymbol{f}_i$. A student computes the new coordinates as $\boldsymbol{y}=F^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$, that is by the dot products $\boldsymbol{f}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$. For which bases is this correct for every $\boldsymbol{x}$?
options: Every basis of mutually orthogonal vectors, of any lengths
Every basis whose matrix has $\det F=\pm1$
Exactly the orthonormal bases: mutually orthogonal unit vectors
Every basis whose matrix is symmetric, $F^{\top}=F$

questions.question: In a three-dimensional space $V$ with ordered basis $\mathcal{C}$, a student takes vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_3=\boldsymbol{v}_1+\boldsymbol{v}_2$ and forms $M=\big([\boldsymbol{v}_1]_{\mathcal{C}}\ [\boldsymbol{v}_2]_{\mathcal{C}}\ [\boldsymbol{v}_3]_{\mathcal{C}}\big)$ to use as a transformation matrix. Which statement about $M$ is correct?
options: $M$ is invertible, because its columns are coordinates in the basis $\mathcal{C}$
$M$ is singular, yet every vector has unique coordinates with respect to the list
$M$ is singular, and coordinates with respect to the list are not unique
$M$ has a zero third column, because the vector $\boldsymbol{v}_3$ is redundant

questions.question: Let $\mathcal{B}=(\boldsymbol{b}_1,\boldsymbol{b}_2,\boldsymbol{b}_3)$ be an ordered basis of $V$ and $\mathcal{C}=(\boldsymbol{b}_2,\boldsymbol{b}_3,\boldsymbol{b}_1)$ the same vectors in a cyclically shifted order. If $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=(1,2,3)^{\top}$, what is $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}$?

Two ordered bases of $\mathbb{R}^2$ are $\mathcal{B}=\big((1,1)^{\top},(1,-1)^{\top}\big)$ and $\mathcal{C}=\big((1,0)^{\top},(1,1)^{\top}\big)$, with vectors in standard coordinates. Find $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}$ for the vector whose $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates are $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=(1,2)^{\top}$.
